p.seg: Therefore, Zhòng Ní said:
"What is necessary is the rectification of names!
If names are not correct,
then speech will not be smooth."
The Great Dao does not name,
but the multitude of things must be named.
Having their origin in non-naming,
then the various forms naturally attain their squareness and roundness.
Names arise from squareness and roundness,
then the myriad names attain what they designate.
One who governs by the Great Dao
will find that names, laws, the Ru school, and the Mo school abolish themselves.
One who governs by names, laws, the Ru school, and the Mo school
will not be able to depart from the Dao.
Lǎozǐ said:
"The Dao is the mystery of all things,
the treasure of the good person,
and the refuge of the not-good person."
Those who are governed by the Dao
They are called good people;
those who rely on names, laws, Confucianism, and Mohism
are called not-good people.
The distinction between good people and not-good people
becomes increasingly clear with each passing day,
and cannot be properly discerned and obtained.
If the Dào is insufficient to govern, then use laws;
if laws are insufficient to govern, then use techniques;
if techniques are insufficient to govern, then use power;
if power is insufficient to govern, then use influence.
When influence is employed, it reverts to power;
when power is employed, it reverts to techniques;
when techniques are employed, it reverts to laws;
when laws are employed, it reverts to the Dào;
Great Dao Chapter
The Great Dao is without form,
yet it names things according to their capacities.
Naming is the correction of forms.
If forms are corrected by names,
then names must not be inaccurate.
when the Dào is employed, there is wú wéi (non-action) and spontaneous order.
Therefore, when exhausted, one seeks the end;
seeking the end reverts to the beginning;
beginning and end follow each other in succession,
without limit.
That which has form must have a name,
that which has a name does not necessarily have form.
If there is form but no name,
it does not necessarily lose its reality of squareness, roundness, whiteness, or blackness;
if there is a name but no form,
one must not fail to seek the name in order to examine its deviation.
Therefore, there are also names to examine forms,
forms to define names,
Names are used to define matters,
and matters are used to verify names.
Examine the reasons why this is so,
and then the correspondence between names and reality,
and the principles will have nowhere to hide.
Names have three categories,
and laws have four presentations.
The first is the name for designating objects,
such as square (fāng), round (yuán), white (bái), and black (hēi);
the second is the name for praise and blame,
such as good (shàn), evil (è), noble (guì), and lowly (jiàn);
the third is the name for analogical description,
such as wise (xián), foolish (yú), love (ài), and hate (zēng).
The first is the unchanging law,
such as ruler and subject (jūn chén), high and low (shàng xià);
the second is the law for standardizing customs,
such as the capable and the base (néng bǐ), similarities and differences (tóng yì);
the third is the law for governing the masses,
such as rewards (qìng), awards (shǎng), punishments (xíng), and laws (fǎ);
the fourth is the law for leveling and balancing,
such as musical pitch (lǜ), measures (dù), weights (quán), and volumes (liàng).
Statecraft (shù) is what the ruler secretly uses,
and the subordinates must not recklessly pry into it;
power (shì) is the sharp tool for controlling laws,
and the subordinates must not recklessly exercise it.
If the ruler has statecraft (shù)
and allows the subordinates to pry into it,
Those who do not understand the profundity of statecraft;
have power,
and cause subordinates to be capable,
but do not understand the importance of power.
The main point lies in first rectifying names and roles,
so that they do not encroach upon or mix with each other.
Only then can statecraft be kept secret and power be held exclusively.
"Name" (míng) is what defines the form (xíng),
and "form" is what corresponds to the name.
However, form is not the same as the rectification of names,
and name is not the same as the rectification of form.
Therefore, form and name
are clearly distinct.
They cannot be confused with each other,
nor can one exist without the other.
Without names, the Great Dao would have no designation.
With names, forms are rectified.
Now that all things exist,
if names are not used to rectify them, there will be chaos.
All names being listed,
if forms do not correspond to them, there will be discord.
Therefore, form and name must be rectified.
Good names denote good,
bad names denote bad,
thus good has a good name,
and bad has a bad name.
Sagehood, virtue, benevolence, and wisdom
Mìng (命) is that which is good;
wányín (頑嚚), xiōngyú (凶愚) is,
that which is bad.
Now, if we take the names of sagehood, worthiness, benevolence, and wisdom,
and use them to seek the reality of sagehood, worthiness, benevolence, and wisdom,
we will not necessarily find it completely;
if we take the names of wányín (頑嚚) and xiōngyú (凶愚),
and use them to seek the reality of wányín (頑嚚) and xiōngyú (凶愚),
we will also not necessarily find it completely.
If good and bad are distinctly and completely differentiated,
even if we cannot fully grasp the reality of things,
we still need not worry about their being confused.
Therefore, it is said:
"Names must be distinguished."
Names are
what we use to compare "this" and "that" and to examine what is empty and what is real.
From ancient times to the present,
none have failed to achieve success by using "this" and to fail by using "that".
Failure results from confusing names and distinctions,
success results from clarifying names and distinctions.
Now, we are intimate with the worthy and estranged from the unworthy,
we reward good and punish evil.
The names of worthy, unworthy, good, and evil
should belong to "that" (彼, *bǐ*);
the terms of intimacy, estrangement, reward, and punishment
should belong to "us" (我, *wǒ*).
"Us" and "that"
Furthermore, there is another aspect of names.
Names are used to discern;
they distinguish between Xián (virtuous) and Bùxiào (unworthy), determining who is close and who is distant;
they distinguish between Shàn (good) and È (evil), determining who is rewarded and who is punished.
If one combines the singular designations "that" and "this" without differentiating between them,
that is a case of names being mixed up.
Therefore, it is said:
"Names and designations
must be carefully examined."
It is said:
"Good ox."
And again, it is said:
"They must be carefully examined."
"Good" is a general term for things,
while "ox" is a specific shape of a thing.
Using a general term to follow a specific shape
is something that cannot be fully explored.
If one were to say "good horse" again,
then "good" would again be connected to "horse".
Then the scope of "good"
would be boundless.
If one were to say "good person" again,
then "good" would belong to "person."
Then "good" is not "person,"
and "person" is not "good";
thus, the names "good ox," "good horse," and "good person" are distinct from each other.
Therefore, it is said:
"The categories of names must not be confused."
The five colors, five sounds, five smells, and five tastes,
a total of four categories,
naturally exist between Heaven and Earth,
and are not intended for human use.
People inevitably use them,
having their own likes and dislikes throughout their lives,
yet are unable to distinguish their categories,
which names properly belong to "that" (彼 bǐ),
and which properly belong to "me" (我 wǒ).
I love white and hate black,
favor the *shāng* (商) tone and reject the *zhǐ* (徵) tone,
like the smell of mutton and dislike the smell of burning,
crave sweetness and detest bitterness.
White, black, *shāng*, *zhǐ*, muttony, burnt, sweet, and bitter,
are the names of "that";
love, hate, favor, reject, like, dislike, crave, and detest,
are the categories of "me".
By defining these names and categories,
all things will be in order.
Therefore, people use measures to judge length,
use capacity to receive small and large quantities,
use scales to balance light and heavy weights,
use musical pipes to harmonize clear and turbid sounds,
use names to investigate the fictitious and the real,
use laws to govern order and chaos,
use simplicity to govern complexity and confusion,
use ease to manage danger and difficulty.
To make all affairs return to one,
and all measures conform to the law.
"Returning to one" means the utmost simplicity;
"conforming to the law" means the ultimate ease.
If it is so,
even the stubborn, obstinate, deaf, and blind
can have their governance be the same as those who are perceptive, wise, keen, and intelligent.
The myriad affairs of the world cannot all be handled by one person.
To demand that one person be capable of handling all affairs,
then even sages would still find it difficult.
Even if there were one person capable of handling all the affairs of the world,
and of appropriately dealing with what is on the left, right, front, and back,
and the matters of distance, nearness, delay, and speed,
there would certainly be things they could not attend to simultaneously.
If there are things that are not attended to,
governance will be lacking.
For governance to be complete and without deficiency,
whether it is big or small, much or little,
each should be assigned its proper share.
Farmers, merchants, artisans, and officials should not change their occupations.
Experienced farmers, established merchants, skilled artisans, and seasoned officials should all be retained.
Then what is the role of those in positions of authority?
Therefore, what is reasonable but not beneficial to governance,
the jūnzǐ 君子 do not speak of;
what is capable but not beneficial to affairs,
the jūnzǐ 君子 do not do.
It is not that the jūnzǐ 君子 delight in speaking,
To be beneficial to governance is something that must be spoken of;
bùdé bù yán;
the gentleman does not delight in acting for the sake of acting,
but if it is beneficial to the matter at hand,
it must be done.
Therefore, what they speak of does not go beyond names, laws, power, and techniques,
and what they do does not go beyond agriculture and military formations.
It's simply about comprehensive business,
therefore the enlightened ruler does not act.
Principles beyond governance
the petty person must speak of;
abilities beyond affairs
the petty person also knows that speaking damages governance,
but they cannot help but speak;
the petty person also knows that ability damages affairs,
but they cannot help but act.
Therefore, what they speak of
reaches the extremes of the distinctions of right and wrong of the Ru (Confucians) and Mo (Mohists);
what they do
reaches the extremes of stubbornness, deceit, bias, and resistance;
it's merely seeking fame,
therefore the enlightened ruler executes them.
An ancient saying states:
"Not knowing is harmless to the gentleman,
knowing does no harm to the petty person.
Skilled craftsmen cannot be harmless in their craft,
the gentleman not knowing is harmless to governance."
This is my letter.
To do good,
making it so others cannot follow,
this is doing good alone (*dú shàn*).
To be skillful,
making it so others cannot follow,
this is being skillful alone (*dú qiǎo*).
This has not exhausted the principles of goodness and skill.
To do good and act with the masses,
to be skillful and enable the masses to be skillful,
this is the best of goodness and the best of skill.
What is valued in the sage's governance
is not valuing his governing alone,
but valuing his ability to govern together with the masses.
What is valued in the skill of artisans (*gōng yáo*)
is not valuing their skill alone,
but valuing their ability to be skillful together with the masses.
People of the present age
desire to be virtuous alone in their conduct,
desire to be capable alone in their affairs,
desire to stand out from the crowd in their arguments,
and desire to surpass the multitude in their courage.
The virtue of acting alone
is insufficient to bring about transformation.
The affairs of being capable alone
are insufficient to accomplish all duties.
Arguments that stand out from the crowd
One must not persuade households;
the courage to defy the masses
is not to be employed in battle.
All these four:
are sources from which chaos arises.
Therefore, the sage relies on the Dao to level their dangers,
and establishes laws to regulate their differences,
so that the wise and the foolish do not abandon each other,
and the capable and the base do not forsake each other.
When the capable and the base do not forsake each other,
then the capable and the base achieve equal merit;
when the wise and the foolish do not abandon each other,
then the wise share equal consideration.
This is the art of supreme governance.
When names are fixed,
then things do not contend;
when distinctions are clear,
then selfishness does not prevail.
That things do not contend,
is not because they are without intention,
but because names are fixed,
thus there is no place to put their intention;
that selfishness does not prevail,
is not because they are without desire,
but because distinctions are clear,
thus there is no place to put their desire.
Therefore, everyone has both intention and desire,
To obtain the same mindset as those who are without desire,
there is a way to control them.
Tián Pián 田駢 said:
"Among all the scholars in the world, none do not reside in their own homes,
and treat their wives and children as subordinates.
Those who invariably travel to the courts of the various lords
are drawn by profit.
Those who travel to the courts of the various lords
all aspire to be high officials,
but do not plot against the lords
are restricted by reputation."
Péng Méng 彭蒙 said:
"Pheasants and rabbits are in the wild,
and everyone chases after them,
because their distribution is not yet determined.
Chickens and pigs fill the market,
yet no one desires them,
because their distribution is fixed."
When things are extravagant,
benevolence and wisdom are compromised;
when distribution is fixed,
greed and baseness do not contend.
The turning of a round object
is not because it can turn that it turns,
but because it cannot help but turn;
the stopping of a square object
is not because it can stop that it stops,
[Bùdé bù zhǐ yě.] It cannot but stop.
[Yīn yuán zhī zìzhuǎn,] Because the circle rotates on its own,
[shǐ bùdé bù zhǐ]; it cannot be stopped;
[yīn fāng zhī zì zhǐ,] because the square stops on its own,
[shǐ bùdé bù zhuǎn,] it cannot be made to turn.
[Hé kǔ wù zhī shī fēn?] Why resent things for losing their distinctions?
[Gù yīn xiánzhě zhī yǒuyòng,] Therefore, because the worthy are useful,
[shǐ bùdé bù yòng]; they cannot be left unused;
[yīn yúzhě zhī wúyòng,] because the foolish are useless,
[shǐ bùdé yòng,] they cannot be used.
[Yòng yǔ bùyòng,] Using and not using,
[jiē fēi wǒ yòng,] neither is due to my use.
[Yīn bǐ suǒ yòng yǔ bùkěyòng,] Because of their usefulness and unsuitability for use,
[ér zì dé qí yòng,] I naturally obtain their use.
[Xī huàn wù zhī luàn hū?] Why worry about the disorder of things?
[Wù jiē bùnéng zì néng,] Things are all unable to enable themselves,
[bùzhī zì zhī.] and unaware of themselves.
[Zhì fēi néng zhì,] Wisdom is not able to be wise on its own,
[yú fēi néng yú,] and foolishness is not able to be foolish on its own.
[Ér zhì ér yú,] Being wise or being foolish,
[hǎo fēi néng hǎo ér hǎo,] goodness is not able to be good and be good,
[chǒu fēi néng chǒu ér chǒu.] and ugliness is not able to be ugly and be ugly.
[Fú bùnéng zì néng,] Now, if they are unable to enable themselves,
[bùzhī zì zhī,] and unaware of themselves,
[zé zhì, hǎo hé suǒ guì?] then why should wisdom and goodness be valued?
[Yú, chǒu hé suǒ jiàn?] Why should foolishness and ugliness be despised?
[Zé zhì bùnéng dé kuā yú,] Then wisdom cannot boast over foolishness,
[hǎo bùnéng dé chī chǒu.] and goodness cannot mock ugliness.
This is the way to obtain virtue.
When virtue prevails in the world,
the poor and lowly will not resent,
the rich and noble will not be arrogant,
the foolish and weak will not be intimidated,
and the wise and foolish will not oppress each other.
This is because they are settled in their proper roles.
When law prevails in the world,
the poor and lowly will not dare to resent the rich and noble,
the rich and noble will not dare to oppress the poor and lowly,
the foolish and weak will not dare to aspire to be wise and brave,
and the wise and brave will not dare to despise the foolish and weak.
This is where law falls short of virtue.
What the world values
it values in the same way;
this is called custom (sú).
What ministers employ
they employ in the same way;
this is called a thing (wù).
If one deviates from others,
custom will not approve;
if one is hostile to the masses,
custom will universally reject.
Therefore, although their hearts are all different,
their actions appear as one;
though their preferences vary,
their resources and uses are necessarily the same.
This is what customs align with,
and what things are adorned with.
Therefore, what is aligned with must be carefully considered,
and what is adorned must be selectively chosen.
In the past, Qí Huán (齊桓) liked wearing purple,
so within his territory, no one sold other colors;
Chǔ Zhuāng (楚莊) loved slender waists,
and the whole nation showed signs of starvation.
The way superiors lead their inferiors
is the reason for order or chaos.
Therefore, if customs are perverse,
governance must correct them;
if things are excessive,
regulations must be established to restrain them.
Those who are burdened by customs
and adorned by things
cannot be involved in governance.
In the past, the state of Jìn (晉) suffered from extravagance,
so Duke Wén (文公) corrected it with frugality,
wearing clothes of only one layer of silk
and eating no more than one kind of meat at a time.
Before long,
people all wore clothes of coarse cloth
and ate unpolished rice.
King Gōu Jiàn (勾踐) of Yuè (越) planned to avenge Wu (吳)
and wanted his people to be brave,
He encountered an angry frog on the road and saluted it from his carriage.
After several years,
the people, both old and young,
facing the enemy,
did not avoid even boiling water or fire.
The difficulty of those in positions of authority
is verified in this way.
The sage kings knew that the people's emotions were easily stirred,
so they created music to harmonize them,
and established rites to regulate them.
Those below were not allowed to use their personal preferences,
therefore, rites and music alone prevailed.
When rites and music alone prevail,
then selfish desires are diminished and abandoned;
when selfish desires are diminished and abandoned,
then encountering the wise and encountering the foolish are the same.
If governing well depended on encountering the wise,
and chaos depended on encountering the foolish,
then order and disorder would depend on the wise and the foolish,
and not be connected to rites and music.
In that case, the methods of the sages
would perish along with the sage rulers.
The laws of a well-ordered world,
established to be easily passed down through generations but not employed,
would result in more disorder and less order.
If there is more disorder and less order,
then the wise will have nothing to be valued for,
I am truly insignificant.
If one holds a position of power and influence,
even if one is unworthy,
one need not worry that things will not be drawn to oneself.
If one is in poverty and low status,
one need not worry that things will not be estranged from oneself.
Closeness and distance depend on power and profit,
and not on unworthiness or benevolence and worthiness.
I also dare not rely on this as a natural principle of Heaven, or as a natural phenomenon of Earth.
Now, in this world,
the unworthy are truly many,
while the benevolent and worthy are truly few.
The desire for profit
is especially strong in the unworthy;
the sense of integrity and shame
is particularly abundant in the benevolent and worthy.
Now, if we use propriety and righteousness to attract the benevolent and worthy,
the benevolent and worthy we obtain
are not even one in ten thousand.
If we use fame and profit to attract the unworthy,
the unworthy we obtain
are everywhere.
Therefore, it is said:
"Propriety and righteousness cultivate the gentleman,
who may not necessarily require propriety and righteousness;
fame and profit govern the petty person,
who cannot be without fame and profit."
Rewards and punishments are
the affairs of the ruler;
upholding one's duty and demonstrating ability are
the tasks of the ministers.
The ruler assesses merit and promotes or demotes accordingly,
therefore there are rewards and punishments;
ministers are each cautious in their responsibilities,
therefore there is upholding one's duty and demonstrating ability.
The ruler should not interfere with the tasks of the ministers,
and the ministers should not encroach upon the affairs of the ruler.
When superiors and inferiors do not encroach upon each other's affairs,
it is called rectifying names.
When names are rectified, the laws are obeyed.
Receiving the myriad things and sorting them out,
distinguishing what is within the seas and making sure they are not mixed up,
seeing insult without being disgraced,
seeing promotion without being arrogant,
suppressing violence and stopping war,
saving the world from strife.
This is the virtue of a benevolent ruler,
one worthy to be a leader.
Upholding one's duty and dividing tasks so they are not confused,
being cautious in one's responsibilities and without selfishness,
with hunger or satiety, one heart;
with slander or praise, the same considerations;
rewards are not forgotten,
punishments are not resented.
This is the principle of dwelling in a lowly position,
which can be applied to being a person.
In the world, there are those who gain reality through reputation,
and also those who lose reality through reputation.
King Xuān of Zhōu (Zhōu Xuān Wáng) was like this when shooting arrows;
he liked it when people said he was able to use a strong bow.
In reality, what he used was no more than two *shí* [a unit of weight],
and when he showed it to his attendants,
they all drew and tested it.
They stopped halfway,
and all said:
"It's no less than nine *shí*.
Who but the Great King could use this?"
King Xuān (Xuān Wáng) was pleased with this.
Therefore, King Xuān (Xuān Wáng) used no more than three *shí*,
but for his whole life, he thought he used nine *shí*.
Three *shí* is the reality,
nine *shí* is the reputation.
King Xuān (Xuān Wáng) was pleased with the reputation and lost the reality.
In Qí, there was a man named Old Huáng (Huáng Gōng)
who liked to be humble.
He had two daughters,
both of whom were national beauties.
Because of their beauty,
he often humbly declined and disparaged them,
saying they were ugly and bad.
The reputation of her ugliness spread far and wide,
and as the years passed, no one in the country sought to marry her.
At that time, there was a widower in Wèi,
who ventured to marry her,
and she was indeed a beauty of the country.
Then he said:
"Huáng Gōng was fond of being humble,
therefore he denigrated his daughter.
If (the elder sister) is not beautiful, the younger sister must be beautiful."
Thereupon, people vied to court her with gifts,
and she was also a beauty of the country.
"Beauty of the country" is the reality,
"ugliness" is the reputation.
This is a case of obtaining the reality by going against the reputation.
A man from Chǔ carrying mountain pheasants,
a passerby asked:
"What kind of bird is that?"
The pheasant carrier deceived him, saying:
"It is a phoenix."
The passerby said:
"I have heard of phoenixes,
and now I see one directly.
Are you selling it?"
He said:
"Yes."
Then he offered ten gold coins,
but he (the carrier) would not give it up.
Qǐng jiā bèi, [Please double it,]
nǎi yǔ zhī. [then give it to him.]
Jiāng yù xiàn Chǔ wáng, [He was about to present it to King Chǔ,]
jīng sù ér niǎo sǐ. [but after a night, the bird died.]
Lù rén bù huáng xī jīn, [Passersby didn't bother regretting the gold,]
wéi hèn bùdé yǐ xiàn Chǔ wáng. [they only regretted not being able to present it to King Chǔ.]
Guó rén chuán zhī, [The people of the country spread the story,]
xián yǐwéi zhēn fènghuáng, [everyone thought it was a real phoenix,]
guì yù yǐ xiàn zhī. [and eagerly wanted to present it.]
Suì wén Chǔ wáng. [It eventually reached King Chǔ's ears.]
Gǎn qí yù xiàn yú jǐ, [Moved by their desire to present it to him,]
zhào ér hòu cì zhī, [he summoned him and generously rewarded him,]
guò yú mǎi niǎo zhī jīn shí bèi. [more than ten times the money he used to buy the bird.]
Wèi tián fù yǒu gēng yú yě zhě, [A Wèi farmer was plowing in the fields,]
dé bǎo yù jìng chǐ. [and found a precious jade one foot in diameter.]
Fú zhī qí yù yě, [He didn't know it was jade,]
yǐ gào línrén. [and told his neighbor about it.]
Línrén yīn yù tú zhī, [The neighbor secretly wanted to take it,]
wèi zhī yuē: [and said to him:]
"Guài shí yě. [It's a strange stone.]
Xù zhī, [Keeping it,]
fú lì qí jiā, [will not benefit your family,]
fú rú fù zhī." [it's better to get rid of it."]
Tián fù suī yí, [Although the farmer was suspicious,]
yóu lù yǐ guī. [he still took it home.]
Zhì yú wǔ xià, [He placed it under the eaves,]
qí yè yù míng, [that night, the jade shone,]
A light shone in the room,
and the peasant Tiánfù considered his home to be greatly threatened.
He then told his neighbors.
He said:
"This is a sign of a monster;
quickly discard it,
and the misfortune can be averted."
Thereupon, he hastily discarded it in a remote field.
Before long, a neighbor stole it
and presented it to the King of Wèi.
The King of Wèi summoned a jade craftsman to appraise it.
The jade craftsman looked at it,
bowed twice, and stood,
venturing to congratulate the king on the jade:
"Your Majesty has obtained a treasure of the world;
I have never seen such a thing."
The king asked the price,
and the jade craftsman said:
"There is no price that can match it.
The capital of five cities
would barely suffice for a single viewing."
The King of Wèi immediately bestowed upon the person who presented the jade a thousand gold coins
and a perpetual salary equivalent to that of a senior grand master.
Throughout the myriad miles of the world, there is right and wrong;
I dare not deceive anyone about what I believe;
what is right is always right,
and what is wrong is always wrong,
This is also what I believe.
However, that which is "right" is often right,
but there are times when it should not be used.
That which is "wrong" is often wrong,
but there are times when it must be done.
Therefore, using what is right and losing what one has occurs.
Doing what is wrong and gaining what one has occurs.
The principles of right and wrong are different,
and they alternately flourish and decline,
turning them to my use.
Then where does right and wrong reside?
Observe the success of Yáo 堯, Shùn 舜, Tāng 湯, and Wǔ 武,
sometimes they followed, sometimes they opposed,
and they prospered when they gained the right time.
The failure of Jié 桀, Zhòu 紂, Yōu 幽, and Lì 厲,
sometimes they were right, sometimes they were wrong,
and they perished when they lost the right time.
The hegemony of the Five Hegemons was also like this.
The Duke of Sòng 宋 fought against the people of Chǔ 楚 at Hóng 泓.
Gōngzǐ Mùyí 公子目夷 said:
"The Chǔ forces are numerous and ours are few,
please let us attack them before they have all crossed the river."
The Duke of Sòng 宋 said:
"No!
I have heard that one does not strike when the ranks are not formed.
Although I am the remnant of a perished state,
I dare not do such a thing."
Having been defeated in battle,
the people of Chǔ captured Duke Sòng.
The people of Qí murdered Duke Xiāng,
and installed Gōngsūn Wúzhī.
Zhào Hū and Yíwú escorted Gongzi Jiū to flee to Lǔ,
while Bào Shūyá escorted Gongzi Xiǎobái to flee to Jǔ.
Shortly after, Wúzhī was killed,
and the two Gongzi vied for the state.
Jiū was the one who should rightfully be established;
Xiǎobái entered first,
therefore the people of Qí installed him.
Afterwards, he sent people to Lǔ to kill Jiū,
Zhào Hū died for him,
and he summoned Yíwú to be his prime minister.
Duke Wén of Jìn, due to the slander of Líjī, fled into exile for nineteen years.
Duke Huì died,
he bribed Qín in order to seek to return to the state,
killed Huái Gongzi, and established himself.
This one ruler was upright,
yet could not avoid being captured;
those two rulers were not upright,
yet their hegemonic enterprise succeeded.
If one considers oneself right and the whole world deems it wrong,
then one does not know that one is right;
if one considers oneself wrong and the whole world deems it right,
then one also does not know what one deems wrong.
Therefore, right and wrong follow the judgments of the majority,
and are not something one can understand alone.
Thus, to offend the majority is to be wrong,
and to conform to the majority is to be right.
Therefore, the ruler, occupying a position of power and taking advantage of circumstances,
resides in a place that is considered correct,
so that people cannot disapprove of him.
If he remains in place, things will honor him;
if he acts, things will follow him;
if he speaks, things will believe him;
if he acts, things will model after him.
This is how he resides above things
and governs the multitude below.
There are three things that cause disorder in a state:
famine and the dispersal of the people;
if there is no food to gather them,
there will be disorder;
if governing a state lacks laws,
there will be disorder;
if there are laws but they cannot be implemented,
there will be disorder.
If there is food to gather the people,
and there are laws that can be implemented,
and the state is not well-governed,
such a case has never occurred.
The great Dao declined,
and then there were benevolence, righteousness, rites, music, fame, laws, punishments, and rewards.
These eight are,
the techniques of governing the world employed by the Five Emperors (Wǔ Dì) and the Three Kings (Sān Wáng).
Therefore, benevolence (rén) is used to guide them,
righteousness (yì) is used to make them appropriate,
ritual (lǐ) is used to implement them,
music (yuè) is used to harmonize them,
names (míng) are used to rectify them,
law (fǎ) is used to regulate them,
punishment (xíng) is used to awe them,
and rewards (shǎng) are used to encourage diligence.
Therefore, benevolence (rén) is that by which one generously bestows upon all things,
but also that by which favoritism arises;
righteousness (yì) is that by which one establishes integrity of conduct,
but also that by which extravagance and falsehood are created;
ritual (lǐ) is that by which one performs reverence and caution,
but also that by which laziness and negligence arise;
music (yuè) is that by which one harmonizes emotions and aspirations,
but also that by which licentiousness and dissipation arise;
names (míng) are that by which one rectifies the noble and the base,
but also that by which arrogance and usurpation arise;
law (fǎ) is that by which one regulates the diverse masses,
but also that by which names and roles are violated;
punishment (xíng) is that by which one inspires awe in those who are disobedient,
but also that by which contempt and tyranny arise;
rewards (shǎng) are that by which one encourages loyalty and competence,
but also that by which baseness and contention arise.
These eight techniques,
are neither hidden from people nor do they cease to exist in the world.
It did not manifest itself in the times of Yáo 堯 or Tāng 湯;
it did not escape the courts of Jié 桀 or Zhòu 紂.
If it is applied in the correct way,
then the world is well-governed;
if it loses its way,
then the world is in chaos.
Beyond this,
even though it encompasses the heavens and the earth,
and envelops all things,
outside the way of governance,
it is not what the masses can consume and draw upon.
The sages set it aside and do not speak of it.
Generally, the survival or destruction of a state has six signs:
there is a declining state,
there is a perishing state,
there is a flourishing state,
there is a strong state,
there is a well-governed state,
there is a chaotic state.
Those that are called chaotic and perishing states,
are not necessarily those with tyrannical cruelty;
those that are called strong and well-governed states,
are not necessarily those with force and benevolence.
If the ruler is old,
has many concubines,
few children and grandchildren,
and neglects his relatives,
A country where decline is evident;
where the ruler favors his ministers,
and the ministers love the ruler,
where public laws are abandoned,
and private desires are pursued,
is a country in chaos.
A country that is poor and small,
where the families are rich and large,
where the ruler's power is weak,
and the ministers' influence is strong,
is a doomed country.
These three signs,
do not wait for tyranny, cruelty, or brutality before weakening;
even if it appears to exist,
I must call it a country that is already lost.
Internally, there is no exclusive favoritism;
externally, there are no intimate attendants;
branch families thrive;
the order between elders and juniors is not disrupted;
this is a flourishing country.
Farming and sericulture are timely,
granaries are full and substantial,
soldiers and armor are strong and sharp,
borders are well maintained;
this is a powerful country.
Those above do not overcome those below,
those below do not offend those above;
above and below do not overcome or offend each other;
Therefore, when prohibitions and orders are enforced,
and everyone is without selfishness,
even if they experience danger and hardship,
the state cannot be invaded.
This is governing the state.
Generally speaking, these three indications
do not require might or benevolence and righteousness to be strong;
even if it is said to appear weak,
I would certainly say it is a state that survives.
The rise of a ruler who governs well
must begin with executing certain people first.
Those who are executed first
are not referring to thieves,
nor are they referring to adulterers.
These two evils
are great harms of the moment,
but they are not the root of chaotic governance.
The root of chaotic governance
is when inferiors infringe upon the power of superiors,
subjects employ the methods of the ruler,
their hearts do not fear the prohibitions of the time,
and their actions do not follow the laws of the time.
This is the way to great chaos.
Kǒng Qiū 孔丘, acting as prime minister of Lǔ 魯,
executed Shào Zhèng Mǎo 少正卯 in seven days.
His disciples came forward and asked:
"Shào Zhèng Mǎo was a famous man of Lǔ.
When you, Master, took office, you executed him first.
Isn't this possibly a mistake?"
Confucius said,
"Sit down!
I will tell you the reason.
There are five kinds of people that are evil,
and thievery and adultery are not among them.
The first is to be insightful but treacherous,
the second is to be unconventional but steadfast,
the third is to be deceitful but eloquent,
the fourth is to have a strong memory and be erudite,
and the fifth is to agree with wrong and be generous.
If a person
has even one of these five,
then he will not escape the punishment of a gentleman,
and Shào Zhèng Mǎo possessed all of them.
Therefore, his dwelling was enough to gather disciples and form groups,
his speech was enough to embellish evil and deceive the masses,
and his strong memory was enough to oppose what is right and stand alone.
This is a petty person who is a leader and a hero,
and cannot but be executed."
Therefore, Tāng executed Yǐn Xié,
King Wén executed Pān Zhèng,
Grand Duke (Tàigōng) executed Huá Shì,
Guǎn Zhòng executed Fù Lǐ Yǐ,
and Zǐ Chǎn executed Dèng Xī and Shǐ Fù.
These six men
To have different views but the same intentions
, they must be executed.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"My sorrowful heart is deeply troubled,
I am angry at these petty people."
Petty people forming groups
, this is indeed frightening.
The *Sayings* say:
"Flattering eloquence can deceive ghosts and spirits."
Someone said:
"The ghosts and spirits are intelligent and upright,
who would say they are deceived?"
Someone said:
"Indeed, ghosts and spirits are not deceived,
this is even more the skill of flattering eloquence,
there is nothing it cannot penetrate."
Those skilled at argument, though they cannot deceive ghosts and spirits
, can deceive people
, this is clear.
They probe people's minds,
gauge people's desires,
cater to people's whims,
and dare not oppose them,
leading people into wickedness to seek their own benefit.
People like to hear praise of themselves,
they are good at exaggerating it,
hate to hear of their own faults,
They are skilled at disguising themselves.
They grasp [the situation] from the space between the eyebrows and eyelashes,
and cater to it before words and actions even begin.
Common people of the world are pleased when they hear praise,
and sad when they hear slander.
This is the general sentiment of the masses.
They rejoice when someone agrees with them,
and become angry when someone disagrees with them.
This is the general human condition.
Therefore, flatterers are good at offering praise,
and good at being compliant.
When people say yes,
they also say yes;
when people say no,
they also say no.
They follow what people love,
and go along with what people hate.
Therefore, even though an enlightened ruler can accept uprightness,
he may not necessarily become close to the upright;
even though he can keep flatterers at a distance,
he may not necessarily be able to estrange himself from flatterers.
Therefore, even though Shùn 舜 and Yǔ 禹 were able to avoid using flatterers,
they may not necessarily have hated flatterers.
A saying goes:
"Flattery and eloquence confuse things."
That Shùn 舜 and Yǔ 禹 were unable to hate [flatterers] is
something that must be carefully examined.
The *Yǔ* 語 [Discourses] says:
“To detest purple usurping the place of vermilion,
to detest sharp tongues that overthrow states and families.”
These words are truly frightening,
yet one may fail to grasp them throughout their life,
and peril and ruin will follow on their heels.
*Lǎozǐ* said:
“Govern the state with governance,
use unconventional tactics in warfare,
and win the world by non-interference.”
Governance (*zhèng*) refers to names and laws.
To govern a state with names and laws
is to ensure that nothing can disrupt it.
Unconventional tactics (*qí*) refers to stratagems and power.
To employ stratagems and power in warfare
is to ensure that nothing can oppose it.
If one can employ names, laws, stratagems and power to correct and restrain cruel and violent impulses,
then one will have no need to act.
If one has no need to act,
then one will gain the world.
Therefore, if governance is lost, then rely on laws;
if laws are lost, then rely on military force,
in order to seek non-interference,
not to seek strength.
If you seek strength,
then the weak will be able to overcome you.
*Lǎozǐ* said:
"If the people do not fear death,
how can you use death to frighten them!"
The reason why the common people do not fear death
is due to excessive punishments.
When punishments are excessive,
the people cannot rely on their lives.
When life has nothing to rely on,
they view the ruler's authority as nothing.
When punishments are moderate,
the people fear death.
They fear death
because life is enjoyable.
Knowing that life is enjoyable,
therefore, you can use death to frighten them.
This is what the ruler should hold onto,
and what the ministers should be cautious of.
Tián Zǐ was reading a book
and said:
"In the time of Yáo, there was great peace."
Sòng Zǐ said:
"Was this achieved by the sage's governance?"
Péng Méng, who was present,
stepped forward out of turn and replied:
"It was achieved by the governance of sage laws,
not by the governance of a sage."
Sòng Zǐ said:
"What is the difference between a sage and sage laws?"
Péng Méng said:
"Your confusion regarding names is extreme!
A sage originates from oneself;
a sage's laws originate from self-governance.
Governance comes from oneself,
but oneself is not governance.
One can produce governance,
but governance is not oneself.
Therefore, the governance of a sage
is governance by an individual;
the governance of a sage's laws
means there is nothing left ungoverned.
This is a benefit for ten thousand generations,
and only a sage can encompass it."
Sòng Ziyóu was perplexed
and questioned Tiánzi about it.
Tiánzi said:
"Péng's words are correct."
A village elder in Zhuāng,
nicknamed his eldest son "Thief" (Dào),
and his youngest son "Assault" (Ōu).
When "Thief" was walking,
his father chased after him, shouting,
saying,
"Thief!
Thief!"
An officer heard this
Thereupon they bound him.
His father shouted and cursed the officer,
but in his haste, his voice faltered,
and he could only say, "Beat!
Beat!"
The officer therefore beat him,
almost to death.
Jì Kāngqú (計康衢), an elder in the district,
called his servant Shàn Nuò (善𤚽),
and his dog Shàn Shì (善噬).
Guests did not pass through his door for three years.
The elder was puzzled and asked about it,
and people told him the truth.
Thereupon he changed the names,
and guests came and went again.
The people of Zhèng (鄭) called unpolished jade "pú (璞),"
the people of Zhōu (周) called an un-dried rat "pú (璞)."
A person from Zhōu (周) carried a "pú (璞),"
and said to a merchant from Zhèng (鄭),
"Do you want to buy a 'pú (璞)'?"
The Zhèng (鄭) merchant said,
"I do."
He took out his "pú (璞),"
and upon seeing it, it was a rat.
Therefore he apologized and did not take it.
Tián Zǐ (田子) said:
"Everyone acts for themselves and cannot act for others,
Therefore, when a ruler employs people,
he causes them to work for their own benefit,
and does not cause them to work for his benefit."
Xià Jǐ (稷下) Master said:
"Excellent!
Tián Zǐ's (田子) words.
In ancient times, when a ruler employed his ministers,
he sought not private affection towards himself,
he sought manifested loyalty towards himself,
and those holding office were necessarily capable,
those facing battle were necessarily brave.
What rewards and commendations encouraged,
what names and laws aligned,
did not come from his own mind,
and did not benefit his own person.
The saying goes:
'Those with meager emoluments cannot be relied upon to manage chaos,
those with light rewards cannot be relied upon to enter difficulties.'
This is what those in positions of authority should be cautious about."
The relationship between a father and his son is such that,
some orders must necessarily be followed,
and some must necessarily not be followed.
To say, "Dismiss your noble wife,
sell your beloved concubine,"
this is an order that must necessarily be followed;
to then say,
"You must not dare to resent!
"You must not dare to think!"
Orders are sure not to be followed.
Therefore, those who are in positions of authority
must be careful about what they order.
Generally, if people are rich, they do not envy titles and salaries;
if they are poor, they do not fear punishments.
Those who do not envy titles and salaries
are self-sufficient.
Those who do not fear punishments
do not depend on survival.
These two are what the state is most concerned about,
yet they do not know the art of preventing them,
therefore orders are not carried out and prohibitions do not stop.
If orders are not carried out and prohibitions do not stop,
then there is no way to govern.
If there is no way to govern,
then the ruler is merely nominally ruling the country,
merely reigning over the people,
and danger and chaos can be awaited immediately.
Now, if being rich is dependent on titles and salaries,
then people will strive to devote their efforts to their ruler;
if being poor is dependent on punishments,
then people will all fear crime and follow goodness.
Therefore, those who governed states in ancient times
did not allow the people to become rich or poor on their own.
If poverty and wealth all depend on the ruler,
then the ruler exclusively controls them,
The people will know where to turn.
When poor, they blame others;
when lowly, they blame the times;
and none blame themselves.
This is the great commonality of human nature.
However, we cannot, because this is the great commonality of human nature,
condemn it outright.
There are also those deserving of sympathy,
which cannot be overlooked.
If we have equal ability and talent,
yet they are rich and I am poor,
it would be admirable if I did not resent it,
but even if I do resent it, there is nothing wrong with it.
If talent and intelligence are equal,
yet they are honored and I am lowly,
it would be admirable if I did not resent it,
but even if I do resent it, there is nothing wrong with it.
The failing lies in not understanding the difference in utilizing power and relying on influence,
even though intelligence is said to be the same.
This is a fault of being unperceptive,
and though it may be a fault of a *jūnzǐ* 君子 (gentleman),
it is also a cause for the *jūnzǐ’s* 君子 anger.
People who are poor resent others,
while those who are rich become arrogant.
Those who resent others
are aggrieved that others do not benevolently extend their wealth to them.
This arises from a situation that is difficult to accept and cannot be accepted,
It is still pardonable.
Those who are proud because they are in a position of power have no suffering.
But to be proud of people for no reason,
is something emotions easily value, but which cannot be valued;
it is unpardonable.
When people see the poor and lowly, they are neglectful and distant towards them.
When they see the rich and noble, they are respectful and close to them.
If the poor and lowly ask a favor of me,
it is acceptable to be distant from them.
But to be distant from them even if it does not harm me,
is because they are deemed of no benefit to my possessions.
If the rich and noble bestow something upon me,
it is acceptable to be close to them.
But to be close to them even if it does not benefit me,
then they will not dare to be close to me.
When the three are independent,
without a reason to be close or distant,
people's emotions will ultimately not be able to avoid easily taking the poor and lowly and the rich and noble into consideration,
therefore, it is called a great delusion.
The lonely, single, poor, and lowly
are those who are jointly pitied in times of order,
and jointly insulted in times of chaos.
Order is not achieved by pitying the lonely, single, poor, and lowly,
it is one aspect of order.
Chaos is also not caused by insulting the lonely, single, poor, and lowly,
it is also one aspect of chaos.
In every matter, if there is order, there is no chaos;
In chaos, there is no order.
Look at the flourishing of the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
and the decline of the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
and that is the proof.
The poor and lowly hope for wealth and nobility is extremely small,
but the wealthy and noble cannot fulfill even that extremely small hope.
What the wealthy and noble despise,
the poor admire;
what the noble take lightly,
the lowly cherish.
Yet they do not fulfill their hopes,
because they do not share their hardships and pleasures.
Even if they do not fulfill their hopes,
it does not harm their possessions.
Now, the myriad people's hope for their ruler
is like the poor and lowly's hope for wealth and nobility.
What they hope for
is to assess the young and old,
to equalize taxes and levies,
to relieve their hunger and cold in due season,
to alleviate their illnesses and pains,
to make rewards and punishments not excessive,
and to employ them at the right time;
that is all,
and it would not harm the ruler.
Yet they do not fulfill these hopes,
because they do not share their labor and service.
Therefore, for a ruler,
It is impermissible not to share labor and rest with the people.
Therefore, the rich and noble may not reward the poor and lowly,
but the ruler must reward the myriad people.
If he does not reward the myriad people,
then he will be unwillingly supported by the myriad people.
If he is unwillingly supported,
then the ruler's position will be replaced.
There is no danger greater than this!
There is no disaster greater than this!
Extraneous Texts
Two wise men cannot command each other,
two nobles cannot rule over each other,
two debaters cannot subdue each other;
it is because their strength is equal and their power is matched.
Relying solely on intelligence,
one will not achieve success;
relying solely on obscurity,
affairs will certainly go awry.
One bright and one obscure,
this is what the masses support.
Yǐn Wénzǐ saw King Xuān of Qí.
King Xuān lamented that his state had few worthy men.
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"If the state were entirely filled with worthy men,
who would be beneath the king?"
The king said:
"Would it be acceptable if the entire country were filled with unworthy individuals?"
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"If the entire country were filled with unworthy individuals,
who would govern the imperial court?"
The king said:
"Would it be acceptable if there were neither worthy nor unworthy individuals?"
Yǐn Wénzǐ said:
"No,
it is because there are both worthy and unworthy individuals
that the king is honored above,
and the ministers are humble below.
Promoting the worthy and dismissing the unworthy
is why there is a distinction between superior and inferior."
Seeking something through intelligence and effort
is like playing chess.
Advancing, retreating, taking, and giving,
attacking, capturing, releasing, and abandoning—
these are within my control.
Playing *bó* (a type of board game) involves utilizing the advantages of strategic passes,
finding paths to complete circuits,
but one cannot control the size of the dice.
That depends on chance.
When Yáo was the Son of Heaven,
he did not wear layered silk,
He did not eat multiple dishes at once;
his earthen steps were three feet high;
and the thatch of his roof was not trimmed.
Numbers:
ten, hundred, thousand, million, hundred million.
Hundred million, ten thousand, thousand, hundred, ten,
all originate from one.
Extend this, and even to hundreds of millions, there will be no error.
When about to battle,
the officials would read the proclamations and oaths,
issuing them three times and emphasizing them five times.
After this was finished,
then they would engage the enemy.
Yáo's Virtue and transformation spread throughout the four seas,
and his benevolence and kindness covered all living beings.
